19       Plaintiff Kimera Labs Inc. (“Plaintiff”) brings this action against Defendants Raj 
20  Jayashankar, Exocel Bio Inc., Alejandro Contreras, and Deb Hubers (collectively, 
21  “Defendants”), alleging misappropriation of Plaintiff’s trade secrets and unjust 
22  enrichment.  See Doc. No. 51.  On November 23, 2022, Defendants filed a motion to 
23  dismiss Plaintiff’s Second Amended Complaint in its entirety pursuant to Federal Rule of 
24  Civil Procedure 12(b)(6).  Doc. No. 52.  Plaintiff opposed the motion, Doc. No. 55, and 
25  Defendants replied, Doc. No. 56.  The Court found the matters suitable for determination 
26  on the papers and without oral argument pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 
27  78(b) and Civil Local Rule 7.1.d.1.  See Doc. No. 57.  For the reasons set forth below, the 
28  Court GRANTS IN PART and DENIES IN PART Defendants’ motion to dismiss.    
1                              I. BACKGROUND                                 
2  A.   Factual Background                                                   
3       Plaintiff, a corporation based in Florida, is “an FDA-registered tissue processing 
4  laboratory that specializes in scientific research focusing on exosome characterization 
5  and placental mesenchymal stem cell exosomes production and optimization.”  Doc. 
6  No. 51 (Second Amended Complaint, the “SAC”) ¶¶ 1, 6.  “Exosomes ‘have broad 
7  application in the medical field,’ and can, among other things, ‘be used to help burn 
8  victims heal by regenerating skin.’”  See Doc. No. 103 at 2 (citation omitted).  Defendant 
9  Exocel Bio Inc. (“Exocel”) is a competing Delaware corporation with its principal place 
10  of business in San Diego, California.  SAC ¶ 7.  Exocel was founded by Chief Operating 
11  Officer Raj Jayashankar, part-owner Alejandro Contreras, and scientific advisor Deb 
12  Hubers.  Id. ¶¶ 8–10.                                                     
13       Plaintiff invested heavily in developing a “proprietary process method of exosome 
14  isolation” in order to produce XoGlo, “the first clinically available exosome product in 
15  the world.”  Id. ¶¶ 1, 32.  Plaintiff also spent “a substantial amount of time, expense, and 
16  effort” creating its customer list.  Id. ¶ 38.                            
17       Plaintiff employed Dr. Melissa Selinger (“Dr. Selinger”) from March 2018 to 
18  October 2019.  Id. ¶ 19.  Plaintiff required its employees to maintain confidentiality 
19  regarding its customer list and its process (the “Kimera Process”) used to develop XoGlo, 
20  and included such requirements in their employment agreements.  See id. ¶¶ 16, 39.  
21  Plaintiff also required Dr. Selinger to “execute a non-disclosure agreement as part of her 
22  employment,” which barred her from disclosing Plaintiff’s trade secrets and its other 
23  confidential information, such as its standard operating procedures.  Id. ¶¶ 19, 42, 63.  
24  However, Plaintiff alleges that Dr. Selinger and Defendants “brazenly and secretly 
25                                                                            
26

27  construes them in the light most favorable to Plaintiff.  See Snyder & Assocs. Acquisitions LLC v. United

28                                                                            
1  engaged in corporate espionage” in order to establish Exocel, a business that “directly 
2  competes against [Plaintiff]” in the exosome isolation industry using Plaintiff’s “trade 
3  secrets and other confidential information [i.e., Plaintiff’s standard operating procedures] 
4  to manufacture and sell” Exovex, a “competing extracellular vesicle/exosome product[].”  
5  Id. ¶¶ 2, 32.  Dr. Selinger confidentially settled with Plaintiff and is not a party to this 
6  lawsuit.  Id. ¶ 12.                                                       
7  B.   Procedural Background                                                
8       Plaintiff initiated this action on December 28, 2021.  See Doc. No. 1.  On April 7, 
9  2022, Defendants filed a motion to dismiss.  Doc. No. 23.  On April 21, 2022, Plaintiff 
10  filed a motion for extension of time to amend the complaint as a matter of course.  Doc. 
11  No. 26.  The Court granted that motion on the same date.  Doc. No. 28.  On May 11, 
12  2022, Plaintiff filed its First Amended Complaint (“FAC”).  Doc. No. 31.  As such, the 
13  Court denied Defendants’ first motion to dismiss as moot.  Doc. No. 33.  Plaintiff alleged 
14  six causes of action for misappropriation of trade secrets under state and federal law in its 
15  FAC and named Defendants along with Craig Evan Winkels (“Winkels”) as defendants.  
16  Doc. No. 31.  On June 6, 2022, Defendants filed a motion to dismiss the FAC pursuant to 
17  Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6).  Doc. No. 40.  On June 17, 2022, Winkels filed 
18  a separate motion to dismiss the FAC pursuant to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 
19  12(b)(2) and 12(b)(6).  Doc. No. 41.                                      
20       On October 20, 2022, the Court granted Winkels’s motion to dismiss for lack of 
21  personal jurisdiction and granted Defendants’ motion to dismiss, both with leave to 
22  amend.  Id.                                                               
23       On November 10, 2022, Plaintiff filed the operative SAC.  Doc. No. 51.  Plaintiff 
24  did not rename Winkels as a defendant, and as such, the action is currently proceeding 
25  against only Defendants Jayashankar, Contreras, Hubers, and Exocel.  By way of the 
26  SAC, Plaintiff asserts the following three causes of action: misappropriation of Plaintiff’s 
27  trade secrets—the Kimera Process and its customer list—in violation of the Defend Trade 
28  Secrets Act (“DTSA”), 18 U.S.C. § 1836 et seq., against all Defendants (Counts I and II); 
1  and unjust enrichment against Jayashankar, Contreras, and Exocel (Count III).  See 
2  generally SAC.                                                            
3       On November 23, 2022, Defendants filed the instant motion to dismiss Plaintiff’s 
4  SAC.2  Doc. No. 52.  The motion is now fully briefed and ripe for decision. 
5                            II. LEGAL STANDARD                              
6       A Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss tests the sufficiency of the complaint.  Navarro 
7  v. Block, 250 F.3d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 2001).  A pleading must contain “a short and plain 
8  statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 
9  8(a)(2).  However, plaintiffs must also plead “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is 
10  plausible on its face.”  Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007); see also 
11  Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6).  The plausibility standard demands more than a “formulaic 
12  recitation of the elements of a cause of action,” or “‘naked assertions’ devoid of ‘further 
13  factual enhancement.’”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (quoting Twombly, 
14  550 U.S. at 555, 557).  Instead, the complaint “must contain sufficient allegations of 
15  underlying facts to give fair notice and to enable the opposing party to defend itself 
16  effectively.”  Starr v. Baca, 652 F.3d 1202, 1216 (9th Cir. 2011).        
17       In reviewing a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), courts must assume the truth 
18  of all factual allegations and must construe them in the light most favorable to the 
19  nonmoving party.  Cahill v. Liberty Mut. Ins. Co., 80 F.3d 336, 337–38 (9th Cir. 1996) 
20  (citing Nat’l Wildlife Fed'n v. Espy, 45 F.3d 1337, 1340 (9th Cir. 1995)).  The court need 
21  not take legal conclusions as true merely because they are cast in the form of factual 
22  allegations.  Roberts v. Corrothers, 812 F.2d 1173, 1177 (9th Cir. 1987) (quoting W. Min. 
23  Council v. Watt, 643 F.2d 618, 624 (9th Cir. 1981)).  Similarly, “conclusory allegations 
24  of law and unwarranted inferences are not sufficient to defeat a motion to dismiss.”  
25  Pareto v. FDIC, 139 F.3d 696, 699 (9th Cir. 1998).                        
26                                                                            
27  2 While the instant motion to dismiss was pending, Plaintiff filed an emergency motion for temporary 
   restraining order, which the Court subsequently converted to a motion for preliminary injunction.  Doc. 
28                                                                            
1       In determining the propriety of a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal, courts generally may not 
2  look beyond the complaint for additional facts.  See United States v. Ritchie, 342 F.3d 
3  903, 907–08 (9th Cir. 2003).  “A court may, however, consider certain materials—
4  documents attached to the complaint, documents incorporated by reference in the 
5  complaint, or matters of judicial notice—without converting the motion to dismiss into a 
6  motion for summary judgment.”  Id.; see also Lee v. City of Los Angeles, 250 F.3d 668, 
7  688 (9th Cir. 2001), overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County Of Santa Clara, 
8  307 F.3d 1119, 1125–26 (9th Cir. 2002).  “However, [courts] are not required to accept as 
9  true conclusory allegations which are contradicted by documents referred to in the 
10  complaint.”  Steckman v. Hart Brewing, Inc., 143 F.3d 1293, 1295–96 (9th Cir. 1998) 
11  (citing In re Stac Electronics Securities Litigation, 89 F.3d 1399, 1403 (9th Cir. 1996)). 
12       Where dismissal is appropriate, a court should grant leave to amend unless the 
13  plaintiff could not possibly cure the defects in the pleading.  Knappenberger v. City of 
14  Phoenix, 566 F.3d 936, 942 (9th Cir. 2009) (quoting Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1127 
15  (9th Cir. 2000)).                                                         
16                              III. DISCUSSION                               
17  A.   Counts I and II: Trade Secret Misappropriation                       
18       1.   Applicable Law                                                  
19       To plead a trade secret misappropriation cause of action under the DTSA, a 
20  plaintiff must allege the following: “(1) the plaintiff owned a trade secret; (2) the 
21  defendant misappropriated the trade secret; and (3) the defendant’s actions damaged the 
22  plaintiff.”  AlterG, Inc. v. Boost Treadmills LLC, 388 F. Supp. 3d 1133, 1144 (N.D. Cal. 
23  2019) (quoting Alta Devices, Inc. v. LG Elecs., Inc., 343 F. Supp. 3d 868, 877 (N.D. Cal. 
24  2018)).  The DTSA provides for a private cause of action for owners of trade secrets that 
25  are misappropriated “if the trade secret is related to a product or service used in, or 
26  intended for use in, interstate or foreign commerce.”  18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(1).  The DTSA 
27  defines “trade secret” as “all forms and types of financial, business, scientific, technical, 
28  economic, or engineering information, including patterns, plans, compilations, program 
1  devices, formulas, designs, prototypes, methods, techniques, processes, procedures, 
2  programs, or codes, whether tangible or intangible, and whether or how stored, compiled, 
3  or memorialized physically, electronically, graphically, photographically, or in writing” 
4  so long as the owner (a) “has taken reasonable measures to keep such information secret” 
5  and (b) “derives independent economic value” from being secret.  18 U.S.C. § 1839(3).  
6  Under the DTSA “misappropriation” is the “(a) ‘acquisition of a trade secret’ by a person 
7  who knows or should know the secret was improperly acquired or (b) ‘disclosure or use 
8  of a trade secret of another without express or implied consent.’”  Cave Consulting Grp., 
9  Inc. v. Truven Health Analytics Inc., No. 15-CV-02177-SI, 2017 WL 1436044, at *3 
10  (N.D. Cal. Apr. 24, 2017) (quoting 18 U.S.C. § 1839(5)).  In sum, the DTSA 
11  “contemplates three theories of liability: (1) acquisition, (2) disclosure, or (3) use.”  Id. at 
12  *4 (citing 18 U.S.C. § 1839(5)).3                                         
13       The Court previously found that Plaintiff satisfied its burden of pleading plausible 
14  ownership of trade secrets regarding the Kimera Process and its customer list.  Doc. 50 at 
15  12, 15.  Therefore, only the misappropriation element of Plaintiff’s DTSA claims is at 
16  issue.                                                                    
17       2.   Analysis                                                        
18       In its prior Order, the Court found that Plaintiff failed to adequately plead 
19  misappropriation because its allegations were “devoid of any factual substantiation of 
20  Defendants’ knowledge regarding the alleged trade secret information.”  Doc. No. 50 at 
21  17.  Further the Court noted that “Plaintiff must satisfy its pleading burden by alleging 
22  how improper acquisition, disclosure, or use occurred or is threatened by each 
23  Defendant.”  Id. (emphasis in original) (internal citation omitted).  Regarding the SAC, 
24                                                                            
25                                                                            

26                                                                            
   3 In applying the Rule 12(b)(6) standard to DTSA allegations, as previously noted, the Court applies 
27  Rule 8’s general pleading standards, which require plausibility as opposed to particularity.  See Doc. No. 
   50 at 12; Power Integrations, Inc. v. De Lara, No. 20-cv-410-MMA (MSB), 2020 WL 1467406, at *17 
28                                                                            
1  Defendants argue Plaintiff has again failed to meet this burden.  Doc. No. 52-1 at 6–11.  
2  The Court disagrees.                                                      
3       The DTSA permits a court to enjoin “any actual or threatened misappropriation.”  
4  18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(i).  Courts distinguish between direct trade secret 
5  misappropriation claims and indirect trade secret misappropriation claims, depending on 
6  whether a plaintiff alleges that a defendant obtained the trade secrets directly from the 
7  plaintiff or indirectly “from someone other than plaintiff.”  See Heller v. Cepia, L.L.C., 
8  No. C 11-01146 JSW, 2012 WL 13572, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 4, 2012), aff’d on different 
9  grounds, 560 F. App’x 678 (9th Cir. 2014).  Because Plaintiff alleges again in its SAC 
10  that Defendants acquired its trade secrets from Dr. Selinger, the Court assesses whether 
11  Plaintiff plausibly alleges indirect trade secret misappropriation.       
12       Indirect misappropriation includes the disclosure or use of a trade secret of another 
13  when “at the time of disclosure or use,” the person “knew or had reason to know that the 
14  knowledge of the trade secret was . . . derived from or through a person who owed a duty 
15  to the person seeking relief to maintain the secrecy of the trade secret or limit the use of 
16  the trade secret.”  18 U.S.C. § 1839(5)(B).  Both state and federal courts in California 
17  have held that a plaintiff must prove more than a defendant’s mere possession of trade 
18  secrets.  See, e.g., Pellerin v. Honeywell Int’l, Inc., 877 F. Supp. 2d 983, 989 (S.D. Cal. 
19  2012); Cent. Valley Gen. Hosp. v. Smith, 162 Cal. App. 4th 501, 528 (2008).   
20       Here, Plaintiff now includes specific allegations describing Dr. Selinger’s 
21  interactions with each Defendant.  Plaintiff alleges Dr. Selinger had informed Defendants 
22  that she executed a non-disclosure agreement and was still employed by Plaintiff when 
23  Defendants acquired Plaintiff’s trade secrets from Dr. Selinger.  SAC ¶¶ 20, 44.  Plaintiff 
24  alleges facts that, if proven, show: (1) Dr. Selinger, as a former employee of Plaintiff, had 
25  access to trade secret information protected by a non-disclosure agreement; (2) those 
26  trade secrets include Plaintiff’s Kimera Process and customer list; (3) Dr. Selinger was 
27  involved in discussions with Defendants about creating a competing business and 
28  product; and (4) Dr. Selinger improperly provided Defendants with access to Plaintiff’s 
1  confidential trade secrets at Defendants’ request and inducement.  See generally SAC.  In 
2  E. & J. Gallo Winery v. Instituut Voor Landbouw—En Visserijonderzoek, the district 
3  court held that allegations of circumstantial similarities in corporate practices were 
4  sufficient to plead misappropriation when accompanied by allegations of “exactly how 
5  defendants improperly obtained the alleged trade secret,” including that the improper 
6  access was given pursuant to a non-disclosure agreement.  See No. 17-cv-00808-DAD-
7  EOG, 2018 WL 2463869, at *7 (E.D. Cal. 2018).  Thus, by providing the Court with 
8  “exactly how Defendants improperly obtained . . . the alleged trade secret[s],” Plaintiff 
9  has plausibly pleaded trade secret misappropriation.  Autodesk, Inc. v. ZWCAD Software 
10  Co., No. 14-cv-01409-EJD, 2015 WL 2265479, at *6 (N.D. Cal. May 13, 2015) (internal 
11  quotation marks and citation omitted).  Moreover, this Court finds that expecting Plaintiff 
12  to provide exactly how Defendants are unlawfully using Plaintiff’s trade secrets would be 
13  unreasonable at this stage of the litigation.  See id. at *1 (“[A]s discovery has not yet 
14  commenced, it would be unreasonable to require a plaintiff to demonstrate the precise 
15  ways in which Defendants may have used their trade secrets, given that Defendants are 
16  the only ones who possess such information.”) (internal quotations omitted). 
17       Therefore, the Court finds that Plaintiff has now adequately pleaded trade secret 
18  misappropriation under DTSA.  Accordingly, the Court DENIES Defendants’ motion to 
19  dismiss as to Counts I and II.                                            
20  B.   Count III: Unjust Enrichment                                         
21       Before proceeding to the merits, the Court addresses which law applies to 
22  Plaintiff’s common law claim for unjust enrichment.  Defendants argue that Plaintiff’s 
23  unjust enrichment claim is displaced by the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act 
24  (“CUSTA”).4  Doc. No. 52-1 at 4–6.  Plaintiff responds that Florida’s Uniform Trade 
25  Secrets Act (“FUTSA”) should apply.  Doc. No. at 55 at 18–20.  Defendants reply that no 
26                                                                            

27                                                                            
   4 The Court uses the term “displacement.” Courts have also used “supersession” and “preemption” to 
28                                                                            
1  choice of law analysis is necessary when both laws produce the same outcome.  Doc. 
2  No. 56 at 2–3.  Although the Court agrees that the choice of law does not change the 
3  substantive displacement analysis, it will apply CUTSA to Plaintiff’s unjust enrichment 
4  claim for the reasons stated below.                                       
5       In California, the test for assessing whether California law or non-forum law 
6  should apply requires a three-step analysis: first, the court examines the substantive law 
7  of each jurisdiction to determine whether the laws differ as applied to the relevant 
8  transaction; second, if the laws do differ, the court must determine whether a “true 
9  conflict” exists in that each of the relevant jurisdictions has an interest in having its law 
10  applied; and third, if a true conflict exists, the court must determine which forum’s law 
11  would be most impaired if its laws were not applied.  Anschutz Corp. v. Merrill Lynch & 
12  Co. Inc., 785 F. Supp. 2d 799, 821–22 (N.D. Cal. 2011); Parrish v. National Football 
13  League Players, Inc., No. 07-cv-00943-WHA, 2007 WL 1624601, at *3 (N.D. Cal. June 
14  4, 2007) (“When there is no true conflict of laws, the forum may apply its own laws.”); 
15  Aldrich v. National Collegiate Athletic Association, 484 F. Supp. 3d 779, 797 (N.D. Cal. 
16  2020) (same).                                                             
17       Plaintiff argues that CUTSA and FUTSA conflict because “CUTSA preempts 
18  misappropriation claims based on confidential information whereas FUTSA does not.”  
19  Doc. No. 55 at 19.  Not so.  As Defendants correctly highlight, “the majority position in 
20  Florida is that FUTSA preempts all extracontractual claims based on misappropriation of 
21  confidential information, even where such confidential information does not rise to the 
22  level of ‘trade secret,’ unless there is a ‘material distinction’ underlying the purported 
23  wrongdoing.”  Doc. No. 56 at 3; compare Jardin v. Datallegro, Inc., No. 10-CV-2552-
24  IEG-WVG, 2011 WL 1375311, at *4 (S.D. Cal. Apr. 12, 2011) (finding CUTSA  
25  displaces all claims “based upon the misappropriation of . . . confidential information, 
26  whether or not that information rises to the level of a trade secret”), with Am. Registry, 
27  LLC v. Hanaw, No. 13-CV-352-FTM-29CM, 2014 WL 12606501, at *6 (M.D. Fla. July 
28  16, 2014) (collecting cases and stating the majority position that “FUTSA preempts all 
1  non-contract claims based on the misappropriation of confidential and/or commercially 
2  valuable information even if the information does not constitute a trade secret under the 
3  FUTSA”), and Mile High Healthcare Analytics, LLC v. Med. Care Consortium Inc., 
4  No. 18-CV-22374, 2020 WL 9460325, at *12 (S.D. Fla. July 29, 2020) (same).  
5  Therefore, the Court concludes that there is no true conflict, and will apply California 
6  state law.  See Erceg v. LendingClub Corp., 475 F. Supp. 3d 1071, 1078 (N.D. Cal. 2020) 
7  (“The first step in [the] analysis asks whether California law and the law of another state 
8  conflict.  If there is no conflict, then California law applies.”).  Accordingly, the Court 
9  again looks to CUTSA to decide whether Plaintiff’s unjust enrichment claim is displaced.  
10       Noting that CUTSA “occup[ied] the field” in California and “[t]he fact that 
11  Plaintiff [chose] not to plead a violation of CUTSA [did] not change the law’s [potential] 
12  preemptive effect on its [common law] claims,” the Court previously found Plaintiff’s 
13  common law claims, including its claim for unjust enrichment, were displaced because 
14  they were “all essentially based on the same factual scenario alleged in its trade secrets 
15  claims: that Defendants received stolen ‘confidential information’ from Dr. Selinger.”  
16  See Doc. No. 50 at 19 (internal citations omitted).  Plaintiff’s allegations in its SAC do 
17  not allege any new facts that provide a meaningful distinction between the wrongdoing 
18  alleged in Plaintiff’s trade secret claims and that in its unjust enrichment claim.  In its 
19  opposition, Plaintiff argues that its unjust enrichment claim should proceed because it is 
20  only based on Defendants’ theft of Plaintiff’s standard operating procedures (“SOPs”), 
21  which “are different from the Kimera Process and customer list.”  Doc. No. 55 at 24.  
22  However, Plaintiff’s allegations underlying its unjust enrichment claim are clearly based 
23  on the same nucleus of facts underlying its DTSA claims.5  This is because in each claim, 
24  Plaintiff alleges that Dr. Selinger was subject to a non-disclosure agreement which barred 
25                                                                            

26

27  enrichment, which are “based on the same nucleus of facts” as claims for trade secret misappropriation.  
   See Doc. No. 50 at 18 (citing Digital Envoy, Inc. v. Google, Inc., 370 F. Supp. 2d 1025, 1035 (N.D. Cal. 
28                                                                            
1        from disclosing Plaintiffs trade secrets and its SOPs.  See SAC 4 19, 42, 63. 
2 || Therefore, Dr. Selinger’s breach of her non-disclosure agreement was the mechanism by 
3  || which Defendants allegedly misappropriated Plaintiff's trade secrets and stole its SOPs. 
4         Accordingly, because Plaintiff's claim for unjust enrichment arises out of the 
5 || alleged misappropriation of confidential information, the Court finds it displaced by 
6   ||CUTSA.  Jardin, 2011 WL 1375311, at *4.  Therefore, the Court GRANTS Defendants’ 
7    motion as to Plaintiffs unjust enrichment claim and DISMISSES Count ITI. 
8   ||C.    Leave to Amend 
9         Here, Plaintiff does not request leave to amend, and further amendment would not 
10 || change the displacement analysis.  Accordingly, leave to amend is DENIED.  See Elite 
11  || Semiconductor, Inc. v. Anchor Semiconductor, Inc., No. 20-cv-06846-EJD, 2021 WL 
12    3042616, at *5 (N.D. Cal. July 19, 2021) (denying leave to amend as futile in light of 
13  || CUTSA displacement). 
14                                     IV. CONCLUSION 
15         For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS IN PART and DENIES IN PART 
16 || Defendants’ motion to dismiss.  Accordingly, Defendants’ motion to dismiss is 
17  || GRANTED without leave to amend as to Plaintiff's unjust enrichment claim and 
18  || DENIED as to Plaintiffs DTSA claims.  Defendants shall file an answer to the DTSA 
19    claims in Plaintiff's SAC no later than May 22, 2023. 
20         IT IS SO ORDERED.

5                            II. LEGAL STANDARD                              
6       A Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss tests the sufficiency of the complaint.  Navarro 
7  v. Block,
250 F.3d 729, 732
 (9th Cir. 2001).  A pleading must contain “a short and plain 
8  statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 
9  8(a)(2).  However, plaintiffs must also plead “enough facts to state a claim to relief that is 
10  plausible on its face.”  Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly,
550 U.S. 544, 570
 (2007); see also 
11  Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6).  The plausibility standard demands more than a “formulaic 
12  recitation of the elements of a cause of action,” or “‘naked assertions’ devoid of ‘further 
13  factual enhancement.’”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678
 (2009) (quoting Twombly, 
14
550 U.S. at 555, 557
).  Instead, the complaint “must contain sufficient allegations of 
15  underlying facts to give fair notice and to enable the opposing party to defend itself 
16  effectively.”  Starr v. Baca,
652 F.3d 1202, 1216
 (9th Cir. 2011).        
17       In reviewing a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), courts must assume the truth 
18  of all factual allegations and must construe them in the light most favorable to the 
19  nonmoving party.  Cahill v. Liberty Mut. Ins. Co.,
80 F.3d 336
, 337–38 (9th Cir. 1996) 
20  (citing Nat’l Wildlife Fed'n v. Espy,
45 F.3d 1337
, 1340 (9th Cir. 1995)).  The court need 
21  not take legal conclusions as true merely because they are cast in the form of factual 
22  allegations.  Roberts v. Corrothers,
812 F.2d 1173, 1177
 (9th Cir. 1987) (quoting W. Min. 
23  Council v. Watt,
643 F.2d 618
, 624 (9th Cir. 1981)).  Similarly, “conclusory allegations 
24  of law and unwarranted inferences are not sufficient to defeat a motion to dismiss.”  
25  Pareto v. FDIC,
139 F.3d 696, 699
 (9th Cir. 1998).

16                              III. DISCUSSION                               
17  A.   Counts I and II: Trade Secret Misappropriation                       
18       1.   Applicable Law                                                  
19       To plead a trade secret misappropriation cause of action under the DTSA, a 
20  plaintiff must allege the following: “(1) the plaintiff owned a trade secret; (2) the 
21  defendant misappropriated the trade secret; and (3) the defendant’s actions damaged the 
22  plaintiff.”  AlterG, Inc. v. Boost Treadmills LLC,
388 F. Supp. 3d 1133, 1144
 (N.D. Cal. 
23  2019) (quoting Alta Devices, Inc. v. LG Elecs., Inc.,
343 F. Supp. 3d 868, 877
 (N.D. Cal. 
24  2018)).  The DTSA provides for a private cause of action for owners of trade secrets that 
25  are misappropriated “if the trade secret is related to a product or service used in, or 
26  intended for use in, interstate or foreign commerce.”
18 U.S.C. § 1836
(b)(1).  The DTSA 
27  defines “trade secret” as “all forms and types of financial, business, scientific, technical, 
28  economic, or engineering information, including patterns, plans, compilations, program 
1  devices, formulas, designs, prototypes, methods, techniques, processes, procedures, 
2  programs, or codes, whether tangible or intangible, and whether or how stored, compiled, 
3  or memorialized physically, electronically, graphically, photographically, or in writing” 
4  so long as the owner (a) “has taken reasonable measures to keep such information secret” 
5  and (b) “derives independent economic value” from being secret.
18 U.S.C. § 1839
(3).  
6  Under the DTSA “misappropriation” is the “(a) ‘acquisition of a trade secret’ by a person 
7  who knows or should know the secret was improperly acquired or (b) ‘disclosure or use 
8  of a trade secret of another without express or implied consent.’”  Cave Consulting Grp., 
9  Inc. v. Truven Health Analytics Inc., No. 15-CV-02177-SI,
2017 WL 1436044
, at *3 
10  (N.D. Cal. Apr. 24, 2017) (quoting
18 U.S.C. § 1839
(5)).  In sum, the DTSA 
11  “contemplates three theories of liability: (1) acquisition, (2) disclosure, or (3) use.”
Id.
 at 
12  *4 (citing
18 U.S.C. § 1839
(5)).3                                         
13       The Court previously found that Plaintiff satisfied its burden of pleading plausible 
14  ownership of trade secrets regarding the Kimera Process and its customer list.  Doc. 50 at 
15  12, 15.  Therefore, only the misappropriation element of Plaintiff’s DTSA claims is at 
16  issue.

19  misappropriation because its allegations were “devoid of any factual substantiation of 
20  Defendants’ knowledge regarding the alleged trade secret information.”  Doc. No. 50 at 
21  17.  Further the Court noted that “Plaintiff must satisfy its pleading burden by alleging 
22  how improper acquisition, disclosure, or use occurred or is threatened by each 
23  Defendant.”
Id.
 (emphasis in original) (internal citation omitted).  Regarding the SAC,

5  misappropriation claims and indirect trade secret misappropriation claims, depending on

12       Indirect misappropriation includes the disclosure or use of a trade secret of another 
13  when “at the time of disclosure or use,” the person “knew or had reason to know that the 
14  knowledge of the trade secret was . . . derived from or through a person who owed a duty 
15  to the person seeking relief to maintain the secrecy of the trade secret or limit the use of 
16  the trade secret.”
18 U.S.C. § 1839
(5)(B).  Both state and federal courts in California 
17  have held that a plaintiff must prove more than a defendant’s mere possession of trade 
18  secrets.  See, e.g., Pellerin v. Honeywell Int’l, Inc.,
877 F. Supp. 2d 983, 989
 (S.D. Cal. 
19  2012); Cent. Valley Gen. Hosp. v. Smith,
162 Cal. App. 4th 501, 528
 (2008).   
20       Here, Plaintiff now includes specific allegations describing Dr. Selinger’s 
21  interactions with each Defendant.  Plaintiff alleges Dr. Selinger had informed Defendants 
22  that she executed a non-disclosure agreement and was still employed by Plaintiff when 
23  Defendants acquired Plaintiff’s trade secrets from Dr. Selinger.  SAC ¶¶ 20, 44.  Plaintiff 
24  alleges facts that, if proven, show: (1) Dr. Selinger, as a former employee of Plaintiff, had 
25  access to trade secret information protected by a non-disclosure agreement; (2) those 
26  trade secrets include Plaintiff’s Kimera Process and customer list; (3) Dr. Selinger was 
27  involved in discussions with Defendants about creating a competing business and 
28  product; and (4) Dr. Selinger improperly provided Defendants with access to Plaintiff’s 
1  confidential trade secrets at Defendants’ request and inducement.  See generally SAC.  In 
2  E. & J. Gallo Winery v. Instituut Voor Landbouw—En Visserijonderzoek, the district 
3  court held that allegations of circumstantial similarities in corporate practices were 
4  sufficient to plead misappropriation when accompanied by allegations of “exactly how 
5  defendants improperly obtained the alleged trade secret,” including that the improper 
6  access was given pursuant to a non-disclosure agreement.  See No. 17-cv-00808-DAD-
7  EOG,
2018 WL 2463869
, at *7 (E.D. Cal. 2018).  Thus, by providing the Court with 
8  “exactly how Defendants improperly obtained . . . the alleged trade secret[s],” Plaintiff 
9  has plausibly pleaded trade secret misappropriation.  Autodesk, Inc. v. ZWCAD Software 
10  Co., No. 14-cv-01409-EJD,
2015 WL 2265479
, at *6 (N.D. Cal. May 13, 2015) (internal 
11  quotation marks and citation omitted).  Moreover, this Court finds that expecting Plaintiff 
12  to provide exactly how Defendants are unlawfully using Plaintiff’s trade secrets would be 
13  unreasonable at this stage of the litigation.  See
id. at *1
 (“[A]s discovery has not yet 
14  commenced, it would be unreasonable to require a plaintiff to demonstrate the precise 
15  ways in which Defendants may have used their trade secrets, given that Defendants are 
16  the only ones who possess such information.”) (internal quotations omitted). 
17       Therefore, the Court finds that Plaintiff has now adequately pleaded trade secret 
18  misappropriation under DTSA.  Accordingly, the Court DENIES Defendants’ motion to 
19  dismiss as to Counts I and II.

5       In California, the test for assessing whether California law or non-forum law

7  of each jurisdiction to determine whether the laws differ as applied to the relevant

9  conflict” exists in that each of the relevant jurisdictions has an interest in having its law 
10  applied; and third, if a true conflict exists, the court must determine which forum’s law 
11  would be most impaired if its laws were not applied.  Anschutz Corp. v. Merrill Lynch &
